subject: radiology
title: Embolisation agents and techniques

steps.tx: Embolic agents are chosen by how long the blockage must last. **Gelfoam** slurry is **temporary**, reopening vessels within weeks, and suits trauma and epistaxis where healing follows. **Permanent** agents include steel or platinum **coils**, nitinol **plugs**, **PVA particles** and calibrated **microspheres** for tumour and fibroid beds. **Liquid agents** such as cyanoacrylate glue and **Onyx** cast the vessel itself and reach otherwise inaccessible feeders. Matching duration to disease avoids both rebleeding and needless infarction.
steps.say: Agents are chosen by how long the blockage must last. Gelfoam is temporary and reopens within weeks, suiting trauma and nosebleeds. Coils, plugs, particles and microspheres block permanently for tumours and fibroids. Liquid glue and Onyx cast the vessel to reach difficult feeders.

steps.tx: Bleeding embolisation follows the vessel to the source. In brisk **upper gastrointestinal bleeding** beyond endoscopy, **mesenteric coils** or particles close the feeder after angiographic localisation. **Splenic embolisation** preserves the spleen in blunt trauma with blush or high-grade injury. Massive haemoptysis in tuberculosis usually arises from hypertrophied **bronchial arteries**, embolised first before non-bronchial collaterals. Severe **epistaxis** failing packing is treated through the **internal maxillary** and facial branches.
steps.say: Bleeding work follows the vessel to the source. Gut bleeding beyond endoscopy closes with coils after localisation. Splenic embolisation saves the spleen in blunt trauma with a blush. Massive haemoptysis in tuberculosis usually comes from bronchial arteries, and severe nosebleeds route through maxillary branches.

steps.tx: Every embolisation trades benefit against tissue loss. **Post-embolisation syndrome** with fever, pain and nausea follows tumour work and needs fluids, analgesia and reassurance rather than antibiotics. **Non-target embolisation** is the feared technical error, so superselective **microcatheter** tips sit beyond normal branches before release. **Coil migration** can infarct downstream beds, while particles smaller than the shunt may pass to the lungs. **Abscess** complicates embolised necrotic tumours, so sterile technique and follow-up imaging are routine.
steps.say: Every embolisation trades benefit against tissue loss. Post-embolisation syndrome brings fever and pain after tumour work and needs fluids and analgesia. Non-target embolisation is the feared error, so microcatheters sit beyond normal branches. Coils can migrate and tiny particles can shunt to the lungs.

steps.tx: Choosing the endpoint decides success. **Stasis** in the target feeder with preserved flow in adjacent normal vessels marks a complete bleeding embolisation. **Tumour devascularisation** is judged by loss of abnormal blush rather than by the number of coils used. **Pain relief** after genicular or musculoskeletal embolisation lags the procedure by weeks, so early imaging should not trigger re-treatment. **Rebleeding** within days usually means an unembolised collateral or recanalised Gelfoam, not a failed concept.
steps.say: The endpoint decides success. Stasis in the target feeder with normal branches preserved marks complete bleeding work. Tumour success is loss of blush, not coil count. Pain relief after musculoskeletal embolisation takes weeks, and early rebleeding usually means a missed collateral.
